newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels widen control over Zaire territory.
newsitem.headline: Rebels widen control over Zaire territory.

text.p: The fall of Zaire's northeast capital of Kisangani, where rebels on Saturday were reported to have seized the airport, would put about 20 percent of Africa's third largest country in rebel hands.

Rebel forces who launched their revolt last October control a stretch of eastern Zaire bordering on Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania some 1,240 km (770 miles) long from north to south and in places 520 km (325 miles) wide.
It is by far the largest single area held by rebels opposed to President Mobutu Sese Seko since he seized power in 1965.
Mobutu, 66, has survived several insurrections with the aid of foreign troops.
About six million of Zaire's population of some 44 million live under rebel rule, according to analysts of the war.
In the early stages, rebel strategy focused on hitting cities and towns with airports in the east to pre-empt a counter-attack from the air.
A much-vaunted government counter-offensive in January failed to stem the rebel advance, despite some air strikes.

Kisangani has been the main rebel target as it is Zaire's third largest city, holds immense symbolic value as a gateway to the east and is on the last navigable stretch of the Zaire River flowing to the capital, Kinshasa.

The rebels control most of Haut Zaire, at 500,000 square km (193,000 square miles) the largest of the eight regions in the country, most of Kivu province to the south and in the southeast a wedge of mineral-rich Shaba, Zaire's second largest region.
Kivu is the most populous region in Zaire with more than five million people but only the fifth largest in terms of area.

The rebellion had its roots in South Kivu, adopted homeland of the Banyamulenge Tutsi group since they emigrated from what is now Rwanda generations ago, and moved counter-clockwise through the cities of Bukavu, Goma and north before fanning out towards Kisangani via Isoro, Kindu, Bafwasende and Lubutu.
The rebels then concentrated on Kisangani but also pushed west of Lake Tanganyika and deeper south into Shaba region.
Their main thrust took them from mountains around Bukavu to the coffee and tea-growing high savannah of the northeast before descending into a dense jungle plateau stretching across Zaire's interior.
The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire have taken over many mining areas including gold and diamond centres where production has helped pay for the revolt.
But most of copper-rich Shaba including Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city and its mining centre, remains in government hands and some analysts believe it will be the next major rebel target.
